title: How can I call you in? (1.2–1.5)
word: How can I call you in?
hookLine: Augustine asks how the God who fills everything can come into him
tomorrow: can a baby who can't talk yet already be jealous?

lines: TO CALL ON IS TO CALL IN.
cards: The doorbell rings, and the living room looks like a laundry basket exploded: cleats by the couch, mail on every chair, last night's pots still in the sink. Whoever's out there, the first reflex is the same. Wait.
Don't come in yet. Augustine has that reflex, only bigger. In the pages after his well-known first line, he wants to call on God, and then he stops.
To call on God, he notices, is to call him in. And the one at the door already fills heaven and earth. So where, in one small, messy person, is there room?

teach.h: DO HEAVEN AND EARTH HOLD GOD?
teach.b: His questions tumble out. Heaven and earth are filled with God; do they hold him? If God fills everything, what's left over once they're full?
Is there a part of him here and a bigger part there? Augustine doesn't solve it with a diagram. He lets the questions stand, then turns them around.

teach.h: I COULD NOT BE, UNLESS I WERE IN HIM.
teach.b: I could not be at all, he says, unless God were in me. Or rather, unless I were in him. The problem was never that God is far away.
A few pages on, the puzzle becomes a plea, and the house becomes his soul.
In Pusey's translation: "Narrow is the mansion of my soul; enlarge Thou it, that Thou mayest enter in. It is ruinous; repair Thou it."
He admits there's something in it that would offend God's eyes, and asks who will clean it, if not God. Look at the order. Not a better house first and an invitation later.
He asks God to do the enlarging and the repairing himself, after he's inside. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: THE CENTURION'S ROOF, AT EVERY MASS.
teach.b: Catholics say something close at every Mass, just before Communion, borrowing a Roman centurion's words from the Gospel: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; only say the word.

how: At Mass, just before Communion, Catholics say words drawn from the centurion in the Gospel, owning that they are not worthy for the Lord to enter under their roof, and asking him only to say the word.

games.q: what does “how can i call you in?” mean?
o: asking the God who fills all into one small soul
asking a guest to wait until the house is clean
asking where God lives on a map of heaven

games.q: the small house — tap the pairs.
p: what Augustine asks God to do
not worthy that you enter under my roof

s: Augustine says you clean up your soul first, then invite God in
he asks God to enlarge and repair the room himself. the invitation comes first.
Augustine thinks God is far away and has to travel to reach him
he says he could not exist at all unless he were in God.
before Communion, Catholics echo a centurion's words about a roof
Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; only say the word.

games.q: your friend says she can't go back to Mass until she's "got her life together." what fits Augustine's small house?
o: go as you are; the repairs happen after the guest is in.
wait until you're sorted; nobody invites a guest into a mess.
go, but keep quiet about anything that's wrong.
games.why: Augustine asks God to enlarge and repair a room that's narrow and ruinous right now. at Mass, Catholics say they're not worthy, and ask only for the word.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, like a door left unlatched. Don't tidy anything first; let your mind be as cluttered as it really is.
If you pray, you can borrow Augustine's plain words, enlarge it, repair it; if not, just keep the hands open and stop straightening up for a while.

wordCard.voice: How can I call you in? Augustine's question in book one: how the God who fills everything could come into one small, ruined room.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 1.2: I will call upon. Augustine notices that calling on God means calling him in.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: come in, and let the repairs happen from the inside, not out on the porch. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Narrow is the mansion of my soul; enlarge Thou it, that Thou mayest enter in. It is ruinous; repair Thou it.
